titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §42–51: field and tenant (xii 63 – xiv 66)
part: Laws §42–51 · field and tenant (Col. xii 63 – xiv 66)
about: Ten laws on farmland worked by someone other than its owner, and on debts that a bad harvest makes unpayable. A tenant who grows nothing pays what his neighbour’s field yielded (§42); one who lets the field go to waste pays and puts it back in shape (§43); a man who took fallow land to break it in owes it ploughed and harrowed, plus a fixed rent, in the fourth year (§44). When the storm-god floods a rented field, who bears the loss depends on whether the rent was already paid or the harvest was to be shared (§45–46), and a tenant who fell behind may bring in another man to work the field (§47). Then the debtor: a flood or a drought year wipes out that year’s interest and suspends the debt (§48); a field pledged to a merchant is still harvested by its owner, who pays the merchant out of the crop — in grain or sesame at the king’s rates if he has no silver (§49–51).

sentences.l: If a-man a-field for tenancy has-taken-out and in the-field grain not has-caused-to-be,
sentences.i: If a man took a field on lease to cultivate and then grew no grain on it,
sentences.n: The tenant laws open. ana irrišūtim ušēṣi, “he brought (the field) out for cultivation,” is the leasing idiom: waṣûm “to go out” in the causative Š-stem, “to make go out.” uštabši is bašûm “to exist” in the causative Š-stem, perfect (the -ta- after the stem prefix, as in imtaḫar) — “he has caused to be,” i.e. he produced; you will meet it again at §49. Harper writes the field eqlam; the stele has the two signs A.ŠÀ, as everywhere in the code — Sumerograms read in Akkadian, as you have seen since §27.

sentences.l: — in the-field work not doing they-shall-convict-him, and grain like its-neighbour to the-owner of-the-field he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall be proved to have done no work in the field, and he shall give the owner grain equal to what the neighbouring field yielded.
sentences.n: ina eqlim šiprim lā epēšim is a verbal noun phrase: “in the field, (of) work not doing” — the charge he is convicted on. ukannūšu is kânum in the D-stem, “they shall prove (it) against him,” the plural impersonal “they” of the court. kīma itêšu, “like its neighbour”: the rent is fixed by the yield of the field next door, so the owner loses nothing by the tenant’s idleness. Note the -ma chain again: ukannūšuma … inaddin, “they convict him, and (then) he gives.”

sentences.l: If the-field not he-cultivated and has-left (it), grain like its-neighbour to the-owner of-the-field he-shall-give,
sentences.i: If he did not cultivate the field at all but left it lying, he shall give the owner grain equal to the neighbouring field’s yield,
sentences.n: Worse than §42: not a poor crop but no farming at all. ittadi is nadûm “to throw (down)” in the perfect, “he has left (it) lying.” Here Harper writes the field eqla-am and the stele agrees: the logogram A.ŠÀ with the case-ending -am spelled out after it, a phonetic complement telling you to read eqlam.

sentences.l: and the-field which he-left with-ploughs he-shall-break-up, he-shall-harrow and to the-owner of-the-field he-shall-return.
sentences.i: and he shall break up the field he neglected with the plough, harrow it, and hand it back to its owner.
sentences.n: Restitution in kind: the field goes back ready to sow. mayyārī is the tilling implement (plural, an adverbial “with ploughs”): Harper translates “hoes”; later dictionaries take mayyārum as a heavy breaking-plough — the exact tool is a guess either way. imaḫḫaṣ “he shall strike” is maḫāṣum, here “to break (the ground)”; išakkak is šakākum, to harrow.

sentences.l: in the-fourth year the-field with-ploughs he-shall-break-up, he-shall-hoe and he-shall-harrow and to the-owner of-the-field he-shall-return,
sentences.i: in the fourth year he shall break up the land with the plough, hoe it, and harrow it, and hand it back to its owner,

sentences.l: and for-10 GAN.E, 10 GUR of-grain he-shall-measure-out.
sentences.i: and he shall also measure out ten kor of grain for every ten bur of land.
sentences.n: A fixed rent for the wasted years. The literal word order is “and 10 GAN.E 10 ŠE.GUR”; the “for” is supplied. ŠE.GUR is grain by the kor (GUR, Harper: 300 KA, roughly 300 litres), and imaddad, from madādum, is “to measure out” grain — the code pays in barley as often as in silver. Harper reads both corner-wedges as the numeral ten and GAN.E as his GAN of 1,800 SAR, about 6⅔ acres (the unit later called the bur, būrum): “ten GUR per ten GAN.” Later study of the field-measure notation reads the first wedge differently: written before the field-sign it counts bur-units, so the line means “one bur,” and the rent is ten kor per bur — ten times Harper’s rate. The signs and the translation here follow Harper; the later reading is the one now generally accepted.

sentences.l: afterwards the-field Adad has-flooded or a-flood has-carried-off, the-loss (is) of-the-tenant.
sentences.i: and afterwards the storm-god Adad flooded the field or a flood swept the crop away, the loss is the tenant’s.
sentences.n: {d}IM is Adad, the storm-god, written with the divine determinative and the sign IM (“storm”) — weather as an act of a god. irtaḫiṣ is raḫāṣum “to flood, wash over.” bibbulum is a crux: Harper takes it as “produce” (the god carried off the produce); later dictionaries read it as a flood (a high-water surge). The ending -um is nominative, which makes bibbulum the subject of itbal: “a flood carried (the crop) off.” Harper’s “produce” makes it the object instead, which the case ending does not support; we follow the flood reading, and the word itself remains rare. bitiqtum, “loss,” is a verbless clause: “the loss — of the tenant (it is),” the -ma on irrišimma stressing whose.

sentences.l: in that year grain to the-owner of-the-debt not he-shall-return; his-tablet he-shall-wet and the-interest of that year not he-shall-give.

sentences.l: If a-man silver from a-merchant took and a-field prepared for grain or sesame to the-merchant gave, “The-field cultivate and the-grain or sesame which will-be harvest (and) take!” he-said-to-him,
sentences.i: If a man borrowed silver from a merchant and gave the merchant a field prepared for grain or sesame, telling him: “Cultivate the field, then harvest and take the grain or sesame that grows,”
sentences.n: A field pledged as security, with the creditor told to farm it himself. eqel epšētim is a field “of works,” already tilled and ready to sow. šamaššammū, sesame (the oil-plant), is written with three signs ŠE.GIŠ.Ì, “grain – wood – oil” (Harper’s ŠE.IZ.NI). erišma, esip, tabal are imperatives — direct speech quoted in the law, closed by iqbišum “he said to him.” Imperatives drop the prefix: erēšum → eriš “cultivate!”, esēpum → esip “gather!”, tabālum → tabal “take away!”

sentences.l: and grain of his-silver and its-interest which from the-merchant he-took, and the-cost of-cultivating to the-merchant he-shall-give.
sentences.i: and he shall pay the merchant in grain for the silver he borrowed from him and its interest, and for the cost of farming the field.
sentences.n: The merchant is repaid in kind, with interest, plus the mānaḫat erēšim, his outlay in working the field. ṣi-ba-zu = ṣibassu, “its interest”: ṣibtum + -šu with t + š assimilating to ss (Harper’s z writes the s). The law protects the borrower from losing the whole crop to the lender, and the lender from losing his costs.

sentences.l: sesame at their-market-rates of his-silver and his-interest which from the-merchant he-took, according-to the-mouth of-the-ordinance of-the-king to the-merchant he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall give the merchant sesame at the going rate, according to the king’s schedule, for the silver and interest he borrowed from him.
sentences.n: Payment in kind when cash runs out — and the merchant may not set the price. maḫīrātišunu, “their rates”: maḫīrum is the market price. ana pî ṣimdat šarrim, literally “to the mouth of the king’s ordinance,” is the code’s phrase for an official tariff; pûm “mouth” is written with the KA sign. Harper renders ṣimdatum “scale”; it is the royal regulation, fixing the price. Harper prints il-ku-u in this line with a plain k where at XIV 40 he has il-qu-u: the stele has the same sign, KU (ku and qu), in both; the missing dot is a printing slip, and the word is ilqû “he took.”
